items.prompt: Order the reasons: why does the injection rule R1 come FIRST?
options: A hostile page cannot be rescued by good corroboration later in the list; suspicion is raised, never lowered — safety outranks evidence quality
items.explanation: First-match-wins means order is semantics: safety first, then evidence sufficiency, then economy — a well-corroborated hostile page is still a hostile page. (obj-15-a)

items.prompt: Input: injection 0.02, sources_verified 2, conflict true, materiality material_breaking. What fires?
options: R3 ESCALATE [source_conflict] — conflict is checked BEFORE the publish default; two good voices disagreeing needs a human
R8 PUBLISH — the change is well corroborated and material
items.explanation: Walk the rules in order: R1 no (0.02 < 0.5), R2 no (2 voices), R3 FIRES. The publish default never runs. (obj-15-a)

items.prompt: What does PARITY testing prove about the canvas?
options: That the canvas is faster than Python
That the two implementations are basically similar

That the JavaScript rules on the canvas and the Python oracle produce bit-for-bit identical actions and reason codes on every gold row — the canvas is provably the decision maker, and the offline twin is not a mock
That Python is the production runtime
items.explanation: 'Basically the same' is where incidents live: zero disagreements is the floor, and it is what lets a receipt carry canvas.execution_id and be believed. (obj-15-b)

items.prompt: Adding a new policy rule requires, in order:
options: Add the rule to BOTH runtime mirrors, add gold rows exercising it, run the parity test, release — four steps, no exceptions
Add it to the JS side; mirror it next sprint
Disable the old rules and A/B test
Ship it; add tests if time permits
items.explanation: The discipline is the same for thresholds and rules: both mirrors, coverage rows, parity green, then release — the receipt history shows the discipline held. (obj-15-b)
